Spruce budworm flight phenology in Maine

Analysis log

Author

JN Candau

Published

27 September 2026

1 Purpose of this document

This is the running log of the analyses of spruce budworm (Choristoneura fumiferana) flight phenology from daily light-trap catches in Maine. Each section records what was done, the choices that were made and why, and the state of the data or the model that resulted. It is updated as the work proceeds; the numbers below are recomputed from the processed data every time the document is rendered, so they cannot drift away from the files on disk.

Code lives in R/, source data in data/raw/, processed tables in data/processed/. The project is version-controlled at https://github.com/jncandau/Maine_Oct_2026.

2 Trap data

2.1 Source

The captures come from the eastern spruce budworm phenology dataset of Fournier, Candau et al. (2027), held in the private repository jncandau/SBWFieldPhenoDatabase and copied unmodified into data/raw/SBWFieldPhenoDatabase/. The workbook Eastern Spruce Budworm Phenology V1.ods holds three tables — Phenology, Flight and References — joined by referenceID. Only Flight is used here.

Flight is a wide table: one row per trapping record, with the captures of each night in the columns mothsDay160 … mothsDay231 (day of year 160 to 231). A record is a site × year × sampling method × sex combination, and carries its coordinates, the reported season total mothCountYear, and a pointer to the source publication. Across North America it holds 763 records; Maine contributes 643 light-trap records and 36 yard-light records.

2.2 Reading and decoding

R/01_read_trap_data.R reads the sheet with every column forced to character, because the day columns mix numbers with two text codes:

Both codes mean missing data (confirmed 2026-09-26). They are treated differently only because of where they occur: - pads every record out to DOY 231, so keeping those cells would invent trap-nights, whereas m only ever appears inside a trapping season. Interior - cells — those falling between a record’s first and last counted night — are real gaps, and are counted in n_gap_nights rather than lost.

The wide table is then pivoted to one row per record-night, and a calendar date is derived from the year and the day of year.

2.3 Selection

Four criteria define the working dataset, all set as constants at the top of R/01_read_trap_data.R:

The year window drops 1961–1967 and 2016. The catch threshold removes a further 230 in-window records; it also removes, without needing a separate rule, every record that reports only a season total and no daily series, and all of 1963–1967 and 2016, where no trap anywhere in Maine exceeded 99 moths.

2.4 Pooling of sex-split records

Two 1980 localities report the male and the female catch of one trap as separate records. Since the trap is the sampling unit, the pairs are summed night by night before the catch threshold is applied, and the components are removed. Both pairs sampled identical nights with no missing values, so the sums are exact.

Pooling matters beyond tidiness: at Bare Island neither sex reached the threshold alone (83 and 78 moths) but the trap caught 161, so the locality re-enters the dataset.

2.5 The resulting dataset

Two tables are written to data/processed/:

  • trap_records.rds — one row per trapping record, with sampling effort, season total and provenance;
  • trap_daily.rds — one row per record-night that was inside a trapping season, holding the count and its status.

The network is a rotating panel rather than a fixed set of stations: most localities contribute a handful of years, and the annual number of traps varies with the outbreak and with the Maine Forest Service’s programme.

2.5.1 Data quality

The following checks are run by R/01_read_trap_data.R at every read. They report problems; they never repair them.

Georgetown Township 1969 is the one record where the gaps dominate: 23 unrecorded nights against 21 counted, over a nominal season of 44 days. The 1980 pooled records were operated on an irregular schedule rather than interrupted. All other retained records are continuous between their first and last night.

2.6 Minimum effort for phenology

A season total above 99 moths says nothing about whether the trap was running long enough, or at the right time, to describe a flight curve. The rule below matches the requirement to the statistic: for a percentile to be identifiable, the sampling window has to bracket it. If more than 5% of a season’s catch falls on the first night, the 5th percentile sits at or before that night and cannot be located; the same argument applies to p95 and the last night.

The criteria are recorded, not enforced: trap_records carries coverage, tail_first, tail_last and the logical usable_phenology, so an analysis that needs only the median can relax them.

Effort itself is rarely the problem: coverage is exactly 1 for most records and the median series runs 25 nights. Truncation is what binds, and it is not a marginal call in the worst cases — East Allagash 1986 took 77% of its season on the final night, Round Mountain 1972 71% on the first.

The cost is concentrated in the sparse years. Sensitivity of the tail threshold, holding the other two criteria fixed:

1987 and 1988 have a single trap each, so one failing record erases the year. Whether that is acceptable depends on the analysis: a pooled site-year model loses little, a year-by-year trend loses the two terminal years of the outbreak collapse.

2.7 Open questions

  • 1987 and 1988 have no usable record. Under the current tail threshold both years disappear from the phenology set. Relaxing the threshold to 0.10 restores 1987 at the cost of admitting series whose flight period is probably truncated; the decision belongs with the analysis, not the reader.
  • Weather resolution. The CaSR reanalysis covers every retained locality (all within 6.3 km of a grid cell) and every retained year, but air temperature is stored 3-hourly, not hourly, unlike the other four variables.
  • Records excluded by the year window. 1961–1967 and 2016 are outside the reanalysis, and are set aside rather than lost: widening keep_years and setting min_season_total to 0 in R/01_read_trap_data.R restores the full 643-record Maine light-trap set.

3 Weather data

3.1 Source

Weather comes from the ECCC Canadian Surface Reanalysis (CaSR v3.2), a ~10 km rotated-pole reanalysis. The two tiles that cover Maine were downloaded from the CaSR download page into data/raw/Weather_Maine/ — 60 NetCDF files, 4.1 GB, five variables in six four-year periods spanning 1968–1991.

The reanalysis window is what fixes keep_years in the trap selection: 1968 is the first year with weather, and no trap in 1990 or 1991 was sampled.

3.2 Extraction

R/02_read_weather_data.R takes the locality-years from data/processed/trap_records.rds, projects the trap coordinates onto the rotated-pole grid, assigns each locality to the tile that contains it, and extracts the grid cell holding the trap for every hour of the calendar year.

Two details of the file layout needed care.

The period files are not aligned on calendar years. Each spans 31 December 13:00 UTC of the year before its period to 31 December 12:00 UTC of its last year, so the final 11 hours of 1971, 1975, 1979, 1983 and 1987 sit in the next period file. Selecting layers by year within a single file silently returns 8,749-hour years; the script reads both files for those years.

The tiles are read separately. Each locality is extracted from the one tile that covers it, rather than merging two 35,064-layer rasters per variable and period.

3.3 The resulting dataset

data/processed/weather_hourly.rds (51 MB) holds one row per locality-year with a nested Weather tibble: datetime (UTC), datetime_est (local standard time, UTC−5 all year), the interpolated Temp, the raw TT, and PR0, FB, P0, UVC.

3.3.1 Interpolation of air temperature

Temperature is stored every three hours, so two hours in three are filled with chillR::interpolate_gaps_hourly(), which fits an idealised daily temperature curve to the daily minima and maxima — hence the latitude argument — and interpolates the residuals. The measured values are left untouched, which is worth verifying rather than assuming:

The deviation at measured hours is floating-point noise, so Temp reproduces TT exactly where TT exists and only fills the gaps between.

3.3.2 Does the weather look like Maine?

Summer temperature falls towards the north, but latitude alone orders the localities poorly. The coolest Julys belong to coastal and island sites — Bare Island 17.2 °C at 44.6° N, Georgetown 17.4 °C at 43.8° N, Steuben 17.6 °C at 44.5° N — all cooler than Estcourt, 21.0 °C on the Québec border at 47.4° N. Any temperature-driven model of flight timing therefore has to carry the maritime gradient, not just latitude.

3.4 Open questions for the weather

  • Temperature is interpolated, not measured, for two hours in three. Any night-level analysis that depends on a specific hour — the temperature at dusk, or hours above a flight threshold — inherits the idealised diurnal curve, not the reanalysis. Aggregates over a whole night are much less exposed than instantaneous values.
  • Local time is a constant offset. datetime_est is UTC−5 all year, so it is one hour behind civil time in summer. A series nested by UTC year starts at 19:00 on 31 December of the preceding year in local time.
  • Reanalysis, not stations. CaSR is a model product on a 10 km grid: the cell holding a trap is 0.7–6.3 km from it and represents ~100 km², so the extracted series describes the neighbourhood, not the trap clearing.

4 Modelled phenology from BioSIM

Alongside the observed catches, spruce budworm seasonal biology was simulated at every trap locality-year with BioSIM, so that observed and modelled flight phenology can be compared on the same dates and the same statistic.

4.1 Model and weather

R/03_biosim_phenology.R calls the BioSIM Web API through the BioSIM R package, which drives a Java client. For each year one request covers the localities sampled that year: BioSIM assembles the daily weather for those coordinates from its own historical station network and runs Spruce_Budworm_Biology on it — Régnière’s process-oriented model of spruce budworm seasonal biology (Régnière 1982, 1983, 1984, 1987, 1990; Régnière & You 1991), driven by daily minimum, mean and maximum temperature.

This is a second, independent weather source: the CaSR reanalysis of the previous section is not what BioSIM uses. Every simulated day in this run came back marked as resting on observed rather than generated weather.

4.2 Parameters

The model takes eight parameters. Seven are left at the server defaults; the two mortality switches are turned off.

Mortality is off because the question here is when the stages occur, not how many survive. With mortality on, only a few percent of the cohort reaches the adult stage, so the flight curve would be estimated from a handful of individuals: checked at one Maine locality-year, the season totals are MaleEmergence + FemaleEmergence = 100% and MaleFlight + FemaleFlight = 97% with mortality off, against 10% and 6% under the defaults.

LastSampleDate and ObservedAI are left unset, so the simulations are driven by weather alone and are not anchored on any field observation of development.

4.3 What the model returns, and what is kept

The output is daily and everything is a percentage of the simulated cohort, quantised in steps of 0.25%. Besides the eight stages (L2o … Adults) it reports emergence, flight, oviposition and death, separately for each sex. Three quantities are kept, each the sum of the two sexes:

Only flight is a daily flux, so only its cumulative curve is a genuine distribution over the season — and it is the series to compare with trap catches. The two stocks are weighted by how long individuals remain in the stage and are kept for context. The sex-specific columns reproduce the both-sexes columns the model also reports exactly, which is checked at every run.

The simulation is repeated ten times per locality-year and the runs are averaged, which smooths the 0.25% quantisation of a single run; percentiles are unaffected by the choice of averaging over summing.

4.4 The resulting dataset

Modelled flight is centred on day of year 190 on average — 9 July — and the central 90% of it spans a fortnight. Pupation runs about ten days ahead of flight, and the adult stock peaks slightly after flight because adults persist once mortality is switched off.

The locality-year medians are spread over six weeks (DOY 169 to 210) and all 227 values differ, so the simulations respond to site and year rather than returning a regional average: 1974 alone spans DOY 182 to 210 across its 21 localities.

4.5 Cohorts that do not finish

With mortality off, a locality-year should end with essentially the whole cohort having flown. Not all of them do: part of the cohort fails to complete development and is dropped, which shows up as a flight season total well below 100%. flight_complete marks the locality-years that reach at least 90%.

Two features of that list matter. It is concentrated at particular sites rather than scattered — Clayton Lake is flagged in five separate years — which points to a site effect rather than to bad years. And the flagged locality-years are later, not earlier, than the complete ones, which is the opposite of what one would expect if the surviving fraction were the fast developers; it is consistent instead with incompleteness arising in cold site-years where development runs late. The flag is carried on all three series and nothing is dropped: what to do with these locality-years is a decision for the analysis.

4.6 Open questions for the modelled phenology

  • The comparison with the catches is still to be done. On the three locality-years used to test the script, modelled flight ran one to two weeks ahead of the observed catch window; whether that holds over the whole run is the next question, and the two tables join on locality-year.
  • Three parameters are undocumented. ApplyAdultMortality, Defoliation and AdultLongevity have no description in the model help and no stated units. AdultLongevity = 0 in particular may be what makes the adult stock persist to the end of the year.
  • Nothing anchors the simulation to observed development. The model offers LastSampleDate and ObservedAI for that, and the Phenology sheet of the source workbook holds average-instar observations — none of them in Maine, but the option exists for a validation elsewhere.

5 Modelled pupation from bayessbw

A second, independent model of development was run over the same locality-years: the Bayesian development model of Studens et al. (kdis19/bayessbw), driven by the CaSR hourly temperatures of Section 3 rather than by BioSIM’s own weather.

5.1 What the model is, and what “pupal phenology” means here

bayessbw fits Sharpe-DeMichele / Schoolfield development-rate curves to laboratory rearing data, in a Bayesian hierarchical form: every posterior draw carries a rate curve for each larval stage plus a lognormal individual-variation term. The fitted posterior is distributed as the R package sbwFieldPheno, whose dev_days() accumulates development hour by hour through a temperature series and returns the day of year on which each simulated individual reaches a given stage.

The laboratory data stop at L6, so the model describes the five larval stages L2 to L6 only. Pupation is the end of L6 — the last transition the model knows about — and the pupal stage itself is not modelled. Pupal phenology here therefore means the date of pupation, not the duration of the pupal stage. This is also how bayessbw’s own weather simulations use the package.

R/04_pupal_phenology.R runs it with the settings below.

Two things about that table matter more than the rest. dev_days() starts accumulating development on the first row of weather it is given, so 1 March is an assumption about the date of post-diapause L2 emergence, and every predicted date moves with it. And because all 100 posterior draws are used, the posterior spread reported below is the model’s own uncertainty, not a sampling error.

5.2 The resulting dataset

Each simulation returns a matrix of individuals by posterior draws. Sorting a draw’s column turns it into that draw’s population distribution, and taking the median rank by rank across draws gives the median simulated population — the summary bayessbw itself uses, written out in full as pupal_population.rds. Percentiles in the table above are percentiles of that population; the posterior interval is built the other way round, from the median of each draw, so the two columns separate individual variation from parameter uncertainty.

They differ by a factor of four: the fitted curves place the population median to within about two days, while the population itself takes nine days to pupate from p05 to p95. Individual variation, not parameter uncertainty, dominates.

The two models were built from different data, fitted by different methods and driven by different weather, and they place pupation within a day of each other on average. Their disagreement at individual locality-years reaches two weeks in both directions, which is the more useful number: it is the scale at which either model’s site-level prediction should be trusted.

5.3 Open questions for the pupation model

  • The 1 March start is an assumption, not a measurement. Anchoring the simulation on BioSIM’s own L2 emergence date instead would make the two models comparable on equal terms and remove one arbitrary choice.
  • One colony of six. NB is used throughout. The other five are one configuration change away, and comparing them would show how much the source population matters against site and year.
  • The pupal stage is not modelled. Getting from pupation to flight needs either BioSIM or a separate pupal development function; the section below measures that interval empirically instead.

6 Model versus observed

R/05_compare_model_observed.R brings the three sides together, one row per locality-year: the percentiles of the nightly catch curve, the percentiles of BioSIM’s daily flight curve, and the predicted date of pupation from both models. All of them are percentiles of a curve over the season computed by the same helper (R/functions/phenology.R), so p50 always means half of the season’s total has happened by this day.

6.1 What can be compared

A caught moth is not the same thing as a flying moth: the trap samples adults that are active, close enough and attracted to light, whereas BioSIM reports the percentage of the cohort in the flight state. The comparison below is about timing, never about numbers.

Two flags decide which rows carry a meaningful comparison, and both are kept in the output rather than filtered away.

Only the first group is used for the statistics that follow. The truncated seasons are shown in the table because their offset is the diagnostic one would expect: a season that starts too late or ends too early pushes the observed median towards the middle of the sampled window, and those rows sit further from the model than the comparable ones.

6.2 Flight

The model is early, but only just: half a day to four days, depending on which part of the curve is compared. That is a much smaller bias than the one to two weeks suggested by the three locality-years used to test the simulation script, and it settles the open question left at the end of Section 4.

The offset is largest at the start of the season and smallest at the end, which is another way of saying that the modelled flight period is longer than the observed one — 14.7 days against 11.0 between p05 and p95. Part of that is real and part is an artefact of trapping: a trap that catches nothing on a night when a few moths fly contributes nothing to the tails of the observed curve.

The average is not the whole story, though.

This is the substantive result of the comparison, and it has three parts.

Both models get the year right. Averaged over the localities sampled in a year, predicted and observed median dates correlate at 0.83 for BioSIM and 0.71 for bayessbw: warm early seasons and cold late ones are reproduced, and the six-week span of median flight dates across the record is not an artefact of which sites happened to be trapped.

Neither gets the site right. Once the year is removed, the correlation across localities within a year collapses to 0.14 for BioSIM and 0.06 for bayessbw. Whatever makes one Maine locality fly earlier than another in the same summer, neither model captures it.

The residual is not noise, and it is the same residual in both models. It has a clear spatial structure — the offset correlates with latitude at 0.49 (BioSIM) and 0.39 (bayessbw), so both run early in the south, and more weakly with the size of the catch (0.28 and 0.17; the two are disentangled below) — and the two models’ offsets correlate with each other at 0.74, locality-year by locality-year. That last number is the informative one. The models were fitted to different data by different methods and, crucially, were driven by different weather: BioSIM interpolates its own station network, bayessbw ran on the CaSR grid extracted in Section 3. A spatial error common to both is therefore unlikely to originate in either weather source. It points instead at something both models share — temperature-driven development with no site-level modifier — or at something neither of them contains, of which immigration is the obvious candidate.

The worst-fitting sites are southern and coastal — the same localities that the weather section found to have the coolest Julys in the dataset despite their latitude. A model that is too early there is a model whose development is running too fast on those temperature series. They are also the localities that catch the fewest moths, which is a second candidate explanation and is separated from latitude below.

6.3 From pupation to flight

The pupal stage is missing from bayessbw and the trap sees only adults, so the interval between them can be measured rather than modelled.

Both models put the median catch about a fortnight after pupation, which is a plausible pupal period plus a few days of adult maturation, and the agreement between two independent development models on that interval is reassuring. The standard deviation of six days is the part worth pursuing: if it is structured by temperature rather than random, it is a pupal development function waiting to be fitted.

6.4 Would a degree-day pupal stage help?

A constant is a poor model of a poikilotherm’s development, so the obvious improvement on the fixed 12.9 d interval is to accumulate degree-days from pupation and predict the catch median when a threshold is reached. R/06_pupal_lag_test.R fits that and compares it with the constant.

The degree-day model wins by 0.08 days out of sample, on 170 locality-years. The fitted base ran to the bottom of the grid, which is the diagnostic rather than a detail: at a base of 0 °C the accumulation is nearly linear in mean temperature, which is as close as the model can come to collapsing back into the constant. Over the whole dataset it stretches the interval from 11 to 16 days, against a residual scatter of six.

6.5 Why no development function would help

A development model can only use temperature, so two numbers bound what it could ever achieve.

The interval does not respond to the temperature the pupae experienced: the correlation is −0.04, where a development model needs a strong negative, and the best smooth function of that temperature explains 6% of the variance. It is instead a property of the site: 64% of its variance sits between localities against 13% between years, and a per-locality constant cuts the scatter from 6.4 to 3.8 days.

Worse for the development explanation, the sign is backwards. The interval grows with July temperature (+0.47) and falls with latitude (−0.39): the warm southern sites, where development should be fastest, are the ones whose catch arrives longest after predicted pupation. A pupal stage would shorten the interval exactly where the data need it lengthened.

6.6 What the long intervals look like

A quarter of the catch, on average, falls after the modelled cohort has finished flying, and that share is what distinguishes the long-interval sites (r = 0.72). It is also a southern phenomenon (r = −0.46 with latitude). The nightly curves show what that means.

The short-interval sites catch their moths inside the modelled window and then stop. At the long-interval sites the catch is displaced: 62% of it falls after the window against 13% elsewhere, essentially none before it, and at Brunswick Township in 1981 the entire season’s catch — 99% — arrives after the model says flight has ended.

The width, though, is unchanged: 11.4 days from p05 to p95 against 10.9 days for the rest. A same-width curve arriving late is exactly what a slower pupal stage would produce, which is why the result of Section 6.4 is worth restating carefully. The problem is not that the delay is implausible; it is that the delay is not a function of temperature. It is a property of the site, and it is largest at the warmest sites, where a development model must run faster rather than slower.

Millinocket in 1980 is the instructive exception: catch through the modelled window and a separate spike a fortnight after it. Two modes are what an influx on top of a resident population should look like, and a systematic search for them across the 170 curves has not been done.

6.7 Latitude, or how many moths were caught?

The offset’s spatial structure could be something simpler than geography: a percentile estimated from a few hundred moths is a poorer statistic than one estimated from twenty thousand, and the sites that fit worst are also sites that catch little. Latitude and catch size turn out to be nearly independent here (r = 0.14 across locality-years), so the two can be separated.

Both terms are significant and mostly independent: latitude carries four times the unique variance of catch size. The next table asks the sharper question — is this about which localities, or about which years at a locality?

A locality’s poor years are not its low-catch years: within a site the offset does not follow the size of the catch. The effect is between localities — a property of which sites, not of how many moths a given season produced.

The two effects add. Latitude is visible at either catch level and catch size at either latitude, and the interaction is marginal (p = 0.049): the catch effect is somewhat stronger in the south. Restricted to catches of 1,000 moths or more, the latitude gradient survives at about 2.2 d per degree against 3.5 d per degree overall, while the catch effect disappears (r = 0.05).

The worst-fitting sites are both southern and habitually small-catch, so their offsets cannot be assigned to either cause alone. Southern localities that caught in the thousands sit far closer to the model.

6.8 Is the catch-size effect precision, or biology?

Part of it is precision. The spread of the offset is about twice as wide at small catches as at large ones — sd 7.4 d below a thousand moths against 4.6 d above five thousand — which is what estimating a percentile from few moths does.

Precision alone, though, produces scatter, not a shift, and a detection threshold — the mechanism that would produce one — makes a specific prediction: it should clip the sparse early nights, delaying the observed start and narrowing the observed curve. The data go the other way.

Small catches carry proportionally more of their catch after the modelled window, not less before it, and their curves are slightly wider. That is the opposite of clipping, and it is the same signature as the displaced southern curves of Section 6.4.

It also sharpens the immigration hypothesis into something testable. If the late weight came from moths arriving rather than from the local cohort, it should matter most where the local population is small — which is what the negative correlation with catch size says — and those late nights should coincide with conditions that carry moths, which the extracted wind fields can be asked directly. The alternative reading is that a small catch reflects a site marginal for the insect, where the local cohort is both sparse and genuinely late; distinguishing the two needs the nightly weather, not more summary statistics.

6.9 Open questions for the comparison

  • The spatial residual is the next problem, and neither the weather nor the missing pupal stage explains it. Latitude is a proxy, not an explanation. The two models run on different weather and make the same spatial error, and Section 6.4 rules out a temperature-driven pupal stage as the missing piece. What is left is what both models share — development with no site-level host, shading or microclimate modifier — and what neither contains: immigration. Section 6.4 narrows it further: the southern catch curves are displaced late by a week or more at unchanged width, so whatever is missing acts like a site-fixed delay rather than a broadening. Section 7 narrows it again, and changes its shape: the observed dates carry almost no latitudinal gradient while both models impose one of about four days per degree, so this is a gradient-slope error rather than a southern site effect.
  • Trap attraction is not modelled at all. The observed curve is a catch curve. Nightly weather gates flight and gates trapping, and neither is in the comparison yet; the hourly CaSR variables extracted for every locality-year — temperature, wind, precipitation — were extracted for exactly this purpose.
  • The comparable set could be larger. Relaxing the tail threshold from 5% to 10% would return 12 further records and the years 1987 and 1988; whether the added truncation is acceptable is a judgement the sensitivity table in Section 2 supports.

7 Is flight synchronous across Maine?

Section 6 leaves both models early in the south, and Section 6.4 rules out a missing pupal stage as the cause. That leaves a site-level effect neither model contains, and immigration — a locality’s catch need not be its own cohort. R/07_flight_synchrony.R tests the second without using weather at all, by asking whether southern catches happen on the region’s dates or on their own. Two predictions separate the explanations: a wave of moths arriving from the north would flatten the latitudinal gradient in catch dates, and at nightly resolution it would make distant localities spike on the same calendar nights.

7.1 The latitudinal gradient

Over the 3.6 degrees of latitude the trap network spans, the observed median catch date moves by 1.7 days; BioSIM moves it by 14.8 and bayessbw by 11.7. The observed gradient is not distinguishable from zero, and it stays flat on the best-sampled records while BioSIM’s stays steep on the same rows.

Averaged over those 13 years the southern localities catch their moths 1.9 days before the northern ones; the model puts them 6.4 days ahead. Seasonal timing across the network is, to within a couple of days, the same everywhere.

This reframes the residual of Section 6. What looked like a southern site effect is a gradient-slope error: both models spread flight across Maine about seven times more than the catches do, and the offset we were measuring is the difference between a steep modelled gradient and a flat observed one. It also explains why both models show it despite running on different weather, and why the worst sites are the extreme ones.

7.2 Nightly synchrony

A flat seasonal gradient is consistent with immigration, but also with a regionally synchronous emergence that the models exaggerate. The nightly curves separate the two: arriving moths should make distant localities spike together.

Over all 887 pairs the median correlation is 0.13 against a shuffled-year null of -0.09, and 20% of pairs exceed 0.5 against 6% in the null. So same-night synchrony is real. It is also local:

Synchrony decays with distance, and the north–south pairs are the weakest of the three types despite having the same null. The best lag is zero days for every pair type, so there is no systematic delay of the kind transport would impose.

That is the opposite of what a northward wave delivering the southern catch would produce. What the nightly data show is nearby traps sharing flight nights — local weather gating flight and trappability — and southern traps sharing few nights with northern ones.

7.3 What this says about immigration

The hypothesis survives at the seasonal scale and fails at the nightly one. The more parsimonious reading of both results is that real flight across Maine is nearly synchronous and that both development models exaggerate how strongly latitude and temperature spread it: the gradient is wrong, rather than the southern catch being foreign.

One caveat keeps immigration alive: arrivals need not be simultaneous across localities, because the wind fields differ from night to night, so weak north–south nightly correlation is not proof of absence.

A second candidate — that the gradient is really topography, since BioSIM was run with elev = NaN and the CaSR extraction carries no terrain — is tested in Section 7.4 below and ruled out.

That leads directly to a test of how much site-specific weather is buying us at all, which is Section 7.6 below: if flight is regionally synchronous, one regional weather series should predict the catches about as well as a model run at each trap’s own coordinates.

7.4 Is the gradient an elevation error?

Elevation is the obvious suspect for a gradient that is too steep. R/03 leaves it unspecified, so BioSIM takes it from its own digital elevation model, and elevation is itself a latitude proxy in this network: the southern localities are coastal lowlands and the northern ones sit above 300 m (median 68 m against 303 m, r = 0.56 with latitude). R/08_elevation_check.R fetches an elevation for every locality from the USGS 3DEP point-query service — 7 to 573 m, median 218 — and asks BioSIM the same question twice, once with its own elevation model and once with the measured value.

Elevation does move the model. Over the plausible range of 100 to 500 m the flight date shifts by -1.8 d per 100 m at Blue Hill Township and +1.5 d per 100 m at Clayton Lake, against a run-to-run noise of about a tenth of a day. The two signs are not a typo: at the coastal locality a higher assumed elevation brings flight earlier, which cannot be a lapse rate and suggests that elevation also enters BioSIM’s choice and weighting of source weather stations — coastal stations at low elevation have cool summers. The mechanism is not established here; what matters is that the model is demonstrably sensitive.

BioSIM’s elevation model is already right at these localities. Supplying the measured value moves the flight date by a few tenths of a day — of the same order as the replicate-to-replicate variation of the service itself — leaves the mean offset against the catches where it was, and does not touch the gradient, which stays near six days per degree against an observed tenth of a day. A full re-run with elevation, one switch in R/03, would not change any conclusion in this log, so it has not been made.

7.5 How precisely does the location have to be right?

The elevation work turned up something that does matter. A modelled date at a coastal locality is not a smooth function of where the point is: displacing the same trap eastwards in steps, with BioSIM’s own elevation model each time, moves the answer by three days inside the first kilometre and then wanders back.

That is not a lapse rate or a distance effect; it is what a discrete set of source weather stations looks like when a point crosses from one interpolation neighbourhood into another. Two consequences. A modelled date cannot be attributed to a trap more finely than a few days at a coastal site, which matters because the recorded coordinates in this dataset carry a stated uncertainty of one to eight kilometres — though that uncertainty does not predict the size of the offset (Section 6), so this behaves as noise rather than as a bias. And a locality must always be queried at its recorded coordinates: an earlier version of this work used a coordinate rounded to two decimals from memory, landed 1.5 km away, and read that as evidence that BioSIM’s elevation model was wrong at the coast. It was not.

7.6 Does site-specific weather help at all?

If flight is as synchronous as Section 7 suggests, a model driven by one regional weather series — a single prediction per year, the same for every locality — should predict the catches about as well as the site-specific runs. R/09_regional_weather_test.R builds that comparison. The regional BioSIM run is one point at the centroid of the trap network (45.64 °N, 69.12 °W); the regional bayessbw run is the same simulation as Section 6.4 driven by the hourly temperature averaged over all localities. Each predictor is given one intercept, fitted on the other years, so a constant bias is not charged against any of them and none is scored on its own year.

Site-specific weather does not merely fail to help. It makes both models worse. Replacing the site-specific run with a single regional series changes the error by -2.22 days for BioSIM and -1.36 days for bayessbw, and raises the correlation with the observed dates from 0.49 to 0.67 and from 0.40 to 0.52. One number per year beats a model run at each trap’s own coordinates.

The last line of the table is the floor: the mean observed date of the other localities trapped in the same year, which is what a perfect regional predictor would look like. At 3.62 days it is only 0.67 days better than regional BioSIM, so the regional run already captures most of the predictable signal, and what the site-specific runs add on top of it is error.

Two caveats on the comparison. The regional predictors cannot capture real site-to-site variation, because they are constant within a year — the result is not that no such variation exists, but that it is smaller than the error the models make when they try to represent it. And averaging temperature before running a development model is not the same as averaging the development of each site, since the rate curves are non-linear; the regional bayessbw run is a model of the average weather, not an average of the models.

Taken with Section 7 this is the practical conclusion of the comparison. For predicting when spruce budworm flies in Maine, the useful signal in these models is the year, not the site; and a phenology model applied at a single trap’s coordinates will be wrong by about six days, mostly because it imposes a latitudinal gradient the moths do not follow. Section 8 turns that finding into a predictive model and measures what it can do.

8 Predicting the nightly catch curve

Everything so far has compared summary dates. This section asks the predictive question directly: given a development model, how well can the shape of a season be predicted at a locality — the share of its catch falling on each night?

Abundance is deliberately not predicted. Nothing in this project forecasts population density, so every model below carries one free level per locality-year that absorbs the season total and leaves only timing to explain. A Poisson likelihood with such a level per group is a multinomial over that group’s nights, so the fitted values read directly as predicted shares, and a held-out locality-year needs no level of its own.

R/10_nightly_count_model.R fits 6 such models to 4,319 trapped nights from 170 locality-years (23% of nights caught nothing) and scores them leave-one-year-out.

Three things come out of that table.

A calibrated regional curve is the best predictor, and it is a usable one: 3.0 days of mean absolute error on the median catch date, a bias of -0.3 days, and 82% of locality-years inside five days — all out of sample, and with no information from the year being predicted.

BioSIM’s raw site curve is worse than climatology. Used as delivered it loses to a seasonal average fitted from other years, on both the likelihood and the median. Giving it a free exponent helps, a shape correction does not, and replacing the site curve with the single regional one helps most. Latitude makes things worse again, for the fourth time in this log.

The fitted exponent on the regional curve is 0.24. That is the quiet headline: the model’s curve is damped almost to flatness, and the shape of the prediction comes mostly from the fitted correction around the modelled median. What the development model contributes is when the season is centred — which year runs early, which runs late — rather than the form of the curve.

Calibration removes most of the spatial structure: the residual’s correlation with latitude falls to -0.12 from the +0.49 of Section 6. A southern excess survives — mean absolute error 3.7 days against 2.5 in the north — so the gradient is corrected on average rather than explained.

8.1 What this model is and is not good for

It predicts timing, out of sample, to about three days on the median and within five days four times out of five. That is enough to say when a flight season will be centred at a Maine locality given the year’s weather, which is the operational question.

It does not predict how many moths will be caught: the season total is an input, not an output. It also does not separate flight from trappability. Nightly weather is absent by design, and the model’s own diagnostics show where that would pay: 23% of nights caught nothing, and the count variance is several thousand times the mean, so the nightly residual is dominated by night-to-night variation that a development model cannot address. Temperature, wind and precipitation at each locality-night are already extracted and would enter this model as covariates without changing anything else about it.

One technical caveat for anyone refitting: the correction spline is a natural spline in days from the modelled median, and its behaviour beyond about 0b115 days rests on few nights — the upturn at the far right of the fitted correction is an edge artefact, not a second flight period.
